title: Truthful witness
hook: no false witness: gossip, spin, half-truths

segments.voice: Yesterday, do not steal, and the quiet thefts tucked inside it: wages, time, credit. Your line was give it back. What did you hand back, even if it was only someone's credit? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-two.

A sentence drifts across a lunch table: she's not really sick, you know. Nobody swore an oath. Nothing in it is quite a lie. And by evening a few people see her a little differently. Some readers hear a courtroom behind today's commandment, a place where one witness could ruin a neighbor's life. The King James Bible gives it like this: "Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour." But Christian teachers have carried it out of the courtroom and into every room where one person describes another who isn't there to answer. The lunch table counts. Today: the truthful witness.

Start with how Proverbs describes gossip: "The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly." Gossip isn't loud. It wounds, and the wound goes deep. Proverbs also lists a false witness that speaketh lies among the things the Lord hates, right beside the one who sows discord among brothers. So a lie about someone is never just a private slip. It splits people apart. Now the harder part: what if the thing you say is true? Christians have thought about that too. The Catholic catechism names a sin called detraction: making known someone's real faults to people who had no need to know, without good reason. The fact is true. The harm is real anyway. Martin Luther, in his Small Catechism, turns the commandment around. It isn't only don't lie about your neighbor. It's defend your neighbor, speak well of them, and put the kindest reading on what they do. Spin and half-truths fail that test, even when every word could be checked. Paul gives the reason underneath it all, in his letter to the Ephesians: "speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another." In Paul's picture, a lie about one member of the body is a lie told to the whole body. A truthful witness, then, is more than someone who avoids lies. It's someone a neighbor would be glad to have in the room when they aren't.

Here's the practice: a fast from talking about anyone who isn't present. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you might talk about today: a coworker, a relative, a name in the news. Notice what you'd usually say. Then try Luther's turn. Find one true thing you could say in their defense, and just hold it. If you pray, you can use an old line from Psalm 141: "Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips." The bell holds the time.
Truthful witness. Someone whose words about a neighbor are true, fair and kind, whether that neighbor is in the room or not.
Your line: speak truly. Today, say nothing about anyone who isn't there, and if someone else starts, offer the kindest true thing you know. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Some Christians learn this commandment in catechism classes and examine their speech by it before confession or in personal prayer; Luther's Small Catechism and the Catholic catechism both apply it to gossip, slander and harmful talk about people who are absent.

myth: if what you say about someone is true, it can't do harm
the Catholic catechism calls telling someone's real faults without good reason detraction: true, and harmful.
Luther read this commandment as asking more than not lying
his Small Catechism says to defend your neighbor, speak well of them and take what they do in the kindest way.
"the words of a talebearer are as wounds."

fork.setup: the lunch table goes quiet, and someone turns to you: is she really sick, or isn't she? what do you do?
options: share what you've heard; it's only a question.
say you don't know, and say something kind and true about her.
fork.reveal: Luther's catechism asks for exactly that turn: not only no lie, but defend your neighbor, speak well of them, and read what they do in the kindest way.

original.note: Hebrew, from Exodus 20:16: a false witness, a witness of a lie.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't lie under oath in court.
what it means: don't twist the truth about anyone: gossip, spin and harmful half-truths included.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 20:16 says ed shaqer, a lying witness; the version in Deuteronomy 5:20 says ed shav, an empty or worthless witness.
recall: gathering in silence, waiting on God

notes: Proverbs 6:16–19 paraphrased: 'a false witness that speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren' among the things the LORD hates.

Proverbs 18:8: the KJV has 'wounds'; many later translations read the Hebrew as 'dainty morsels'. The script quotes the KJV and draws 'goes down easy' from 'go down into the innermost parts'; confirm the reading is fair.

Editor pass: hook's 'first spoken into a courtroom' (an unsourced claim about the original setting) softened to 'some readers hear a courtroom'; teach's 'goes down easy' (closer to modern 'dainty morsels' than the quoted KJV 'wounds') changed to match the KJV, with its screen line; howItsDone 'Christians' softened to 'some Christians'.
Detraction (CCC 2477) paraphrased: disclosing another's faults and failings to persons who did not know them, without objectively valid reason. Confirm.

Luther's Small Catechism explanation (eighth commandment in Lutheran numbering) paraphrased: not to lie about, betray, slander or defame the neighbor, but defend, speak well of, and explain everything in the kindest way. The script avoids naming the commandment's number because churches number it differently.
Trapdoor: Exodus 20:16 עֵד שָׁקֶר; Deuteronomy 5:20 (Hebrew 5:17) עֵד שָׁוְא. Confirm the glosses.
Audit pass: teach's flat 'when you lie about one member... you're lying to the whole body' (narrator asserting a moral claim) reframed as Paul's picture.
